personalized:
Professor Ingrid Maes
Editor, European History Quarterly
6 January 2026

Dear Professor Maes,

Please accept this proposal for an article entitled “Voices at the Capitulation: Oral Testimony and the Archive in the Netherlands, May 1945”, a narrative piece of c.8,500 words which juxtaposes six oral‑history interviews with contemporaneous archival records to produce a textured reconstruction of surrender events. The article argues that oral testimony—when situated against documentary provenance—both fills certain experiential gaps and exposes discrepancies that merit careful interpretive reflection.

The oral material comprises interviews conducted in 2023–2025 with six Dutch and British witnesses (full ethical approval received from the University of East Anglia Research Ethics Committee, reference UEA/REC/21/044). These interviews will be paired with archival files from the Nationaal Archief (catalogue reference: 2.10.03.05 fols. 12–19), The National Archives (WO 212/337 fols. 3r–28v), and the municipal archives of Wageningen (Wageningen Archive, accession 1945‑C). On close reading of the file material and the interviews’ transcripts, the article contends that small differences in timing and emphasis—particularly regarding the presence of British liaison officers—reflect not only faulty memory but the different registers of official documentation and lived recollection.

I propose to submit a full manuscript, together with anonymised audio clips and transcripts as an online supplement, within three months. I am prepared to provide a brief data management statement and to comply with the Journal’s policy on supplementary multimedia. The combination of archival folios and oral testimony, I suggest, will model a method suitable for scholars interested in the intersection of memory and document.

I would welcome initial advice about the Journal’s approach to hosting audio supplements and any accessibility requirements for transcripts.

Yours faithfully,

Thomas Beckett
Cambridge / Amsterdam

personalized:
A week can feel like two lives when half of it is spent among labeled boxes and the other half beneath eaves with a kettle on the boil. I spent three days at the archives following a fragmentary trail — TNA: WO 373/94 and an associated letter in WO 373/102 — and then three days in a cottage in Suffolk trying to translate those fragments into scene.

At the repository, the work is tactile: the rasp of a brass catalogue drawer, the quiet intake through microfilm, the smell of paper that has been handled by other hands for decades. There was one sheet (folio 8v) that stopped me in my tracks; a short, administrative note stating a specific time — 04:15, 05-05-1945 — and an instruction that was bureaucratic in tone but human in implication: "advance parties to liaise with local command post". The clarity of hour and action, and the absence of rhetoric, supplies the kind of concrete detail one can rehearse on a page.

Back in the cottage, beneath rain on the eaves and with a kettle scolding the room, I wrote a scene that collapses two hours into a single, taut chapter. The document provides a hinge — a precise time, a route, a terse order — that allows me to stage the meeting between the Allied officer (a fictionalised version of General Foulkes) and a German delegation without pretending I have every private word. One might, if one is cautious, say the file suggests a procedural reluctance as much as a decisive surrender; it would seem that the capitulation was as much negotiated in small, bureaucratic acts as in grand proclamations.

I will of course fictionalise the private moments — the pauses, the tea cup slipping from someone’s hand — but those small archive details lend the scene its pacing and provenance, anchoring invention to lived procedure rather than airy drama.

Editor, The Evening Ledger
7 May 1945

I write from the market square of a small Dutch town—cobbles still damp from last night's rain and the church tower rent but upright—where the German colours were struck at first light. It would seem that the act of capitulation was, when all is said, both formal and strangely domestic: officers signing in a cellar (the clerk's hand trembled, as the margin reads: "für die Ordnung") whilst children peered through shutter slats. General Foulkes's name appears again and again in the field orders I have consulted—on close reading, his signature sits beside a line of German script—and one might infer his presence at the coordinating table though I confess not all will accept that without fuller proof. Troops moved with a muted cadence; the laughter of relieved men did not so much break the air as fold into it. I enclose a short extract from a captured docket—'Capitulation: immediate cessation of hostilities'—which, if authenticated, will alter the narrative of the last hours. I shall continue to verify and report. For now: the square is strangely gentle. Thomas Beckett

The file was TNA: WO 373/91, folio 14r (21-04-1945) — a neat bundle of typescripts stuck together by a decade of dust — and, whilst turning the pages, I paused at a cramped scribble in the margin where one might not expect it. task_instruction: Write a concise practical guide for novice researchers on handling fragile archival documents and requesting reproductions.
task_details: Create a 300–420 word how-to blog post aimed at beginning archival researchers. Explain appropriate hygiene for handling paper, the use of book supports, how to request reproductions and check copyright or fees, and how to record catalogue references properly (give an example). Use the persona's measured tone and hedging language, include one brief anecdote about learning the practice during a rainy archive day, and avoid lists or bullets — present all steps in connected prose.
personalized:
When one first spends time in a reading room, there is an awkward moment of learning how to touch things one recognises as fragile and important. The basic rule, if I'm honest, is to behave as though the paper has a memory; it remembers every finger and tear. In practice that means arriving with clean, dry hands (archives generally prefer bare hands to gloves for modern paper), turning pages from the fore-edge with the pads of the fingers rather than with fingernails, and asking for a book support if a volume will not lie flat. If the clerk offers a polyester strap or weights, accept them; they are there to protect the binding.

When a folio is especially delicate — foxed, brittle, or with loose sewing — signal this to the conservator rather than attempting a risky manoeuvre yourself. On one damp afternoon I learned this the hard way, pausing and asking for a conservator who gently rehoused a trembling bundle and saved me an embarrassment.

Reproductions are often the wise route for further work. Request a digital scan or a photocopy through the archive's standard form, provide the full catalogue reference (for example, TNA: WO 373/94, folio 8v), and note any restrictions. Fees are variable; some repositories include a small digitisation charge, others provide images for free on-site. Always check copyright and donor conditions if you plan to publish an image.

Finally, be rigorous with citation from the outset: record the repository name, catalogue code, folio and date. Such discipline saves you hours later and preserves the provenance of your claim — which, for a historian and a novelist alike, is the difference between guesswork and fidelity.

Boots were tested by a quick stamp and a rueful adjustment of laces; greatcoats were shaken out and their collars sniffed (to judge, it would seem, whether they had spent more nights under canvas than their owners). The muster roll sat open on the counter and served as both inventory and accountability, a paper bridge between regulation and necessity. When tins were issued — stew, bully beef, biscuits — hands closed on them with the small, practical gratitude of people who understood that provisioning was as much a part of winning as any drill. The quartermaster, with a biro behind his ear, made a neat note; nothing theatrical, only work done well.

task_details: Write a 250–350 word blog-style post for an audience of researchers describing how to assess the provenance of a returned diary attributed to an officer in 1945. personalized:
Provenance is the scaffolding beneath every archival claim; without it, even the most resonant diary entry risks drifting into fiction. When faced with a diary attributed to an officer involved in 1945 negotiations, there are a series of pragmatic checks one might perform before allowing the text to anchor an argument.

Begin with the obvious: ownership inscriptions, ex libris stamps, or dedication pages that name a person and date. If these are absent, the folio sequence and sewing pattern can indicate whether pages have been added or removed. Watermarks—visible against angled light—can establish paper manufacture and sometimes narrow a date range; ink composition and ageing (a job for conservation) can corroborate a purported time. Marginalia are particularly telling: the margin note reads sometimes betray subsequent readers rather than the original hand, and the presence of contemporary annotations—turn-of-the-1940s penmanship, shorthand abbreviations—would seem to strengthen claims of authenticity.

Chain of custody matters more than one might assume. A diary that passed through known hands, recorded in accession lists or sale catalogues, acquires credibility; an item that appears suddenly with an incomplete paper trail requires more scepticism. Practical next steps are simple: request a conservation assessment, photograph watermarks, and if necessary, commission limited forensic tests on ink or fibres. None of these measures guarantee absolute certainty, but together they weave a credible provenance or expose gaps that demand circumspection.

task_instruction: Query proposing a comparative archival essay on British and Dutch archival silences and provenance discrepancies.
task_details: Compose a formal query proposing an 8,000–9,000-word comparative archival essay that examines differences in the British and Dutch archival treatments of surrender documents, noting silences and provenance discrepancies. Provide catalogue references on both sides, explain analytical framework, include plan to supply tables of discrepancies as an appendix, and state submission timeline (two months).
personalized:
Professor Anja van Dijk
Editor, Archives and History
6 January 2026

Dear Professor van Dijk,

I propose a comparative archival essay for Archives and History entitled “Silences and Shifts: British and Dutch Provenance in the Records of the 1945 Capitulation”, c.8,500 words, which investigates how differing archival practices and accession histories have produced variant documentary corpora and, consequently, divergent narratives of the surrender. The essay argues that apparent contradictions in secondary accounts often reflect not empirical disagreement but differing provenance paths and curatorial decisions.

The study is founded on parallel examination of holdings in The National Archives (catalogue references: WO 212/337 fols. 3r–28v; WO 211/78 fols. 44r–67v) and the Nationaal Archief (catalogue reference: 2.10.03.05, including the so‑called Duitse capitulatie map fols. 12–27), together with accession files and cataloguing notes from both institutions. On close reading, I shall show that certain items present in Dutch collections were never formally transferred to British custody and that conversely some British administrative drafts were omitted from Dutch accumulations. An appendix will catalogue the principal discrepancies (a simple table listing item, folio, repository, and brief note on provenance) to make the argument transparent.

I will submit the full manuscript and the appendix within two months and will supply photocopies or scans of key accession notes to support claims about provenance. The comparative frame, I suggest, will be of interest to archivists and historians alike and will encourage scholars to attend more consistently to the politics of archival accumulation when writing narrative history.

I look forward to your guidance on any repository‑specific permissions required for publication of selected images or accession notes.

Yours faithfully,

Thomas Beckett
Cambridge / Amsterdam

task_details: Write in the voice of a reenactor portraying a dispatch rider on a motorcycle carrying sealed orders between divisional headquarters and a forward company. Include the physical sensations (engine, mud, wind), a sense of urgency, references to a sealed envelope bearing a catalogue reference or unit stamp, and a concise mention of the intended recipient and capitulation as a potential instruction. Keep the piece paced and sensory.
personalized: The engine coughed into life and then settled into a deep, impatient hum; wind flattened the collar and turned every thought into small, practical considerations — speed, route, the state of the bridge. The envelope sat in a leather pouch strapped to the frame, its seal stamped with a unit number and a catalogue reference that read like a shorthand for consequence. He felt the motorcycle take the ruts and the slicken of mud, the handlebars alive under his gloves. Villages passed in a blur: a church tower, a line of washing, a child staring in plain curiosity. Orders, sealed and heavy with implication, have a peculiar weight that is not measured in ounces. One might later note (it would seem) that the dispatch contained instructions to negotiate a local capitulation; at the moment, the world was reduced to road, throttle and the cadence of the rear wheel on filthy macadam. He arrived, breathless, boots mud-splattered, and handed across the envelope with a brief exchange of eyes that said more than papers ever will.

personalized: Light filtered through canvas in thin, stubborn panes, making a lattice of shadow where stretchers lay shoulder to shoulder. The air was metallic with disinfectant and the sour of unwashed linen; every movement had the economy of necessity. One man — his sleeve rolled to the elbow, hands steady though his round eyes betrayed a tiredness — tied a dressing with a practised knot and consulted a casualty list pinned to a board as if it were a map. 8 May 1945

I confess I did not expect to be so unmoored by the sight of flags coming down. personalized:
There is a peculiar economy to slow research: the small routines you allow to scaffold an otherwise uncertain process. I begin with tea, boiled twice because the first pot is always too eager; I cycle to the archive because the work between pedal revolutions clears an uneasy mind; I end the day in a cottage with the kettle on a low flame and notes spread like fallen leaves.

Today a margin note in TNA: WO 373/91 (folio 14r) — "Hold fast — no capitulation without orders" — felt like a pebble in a pond. I read it in the morning light, bicycle chain still whispering in my ears, and then took it with me to the cottage where the rain kept time with the clock. The ritual of making tea, sitting, and reading the line aloud (as one sometimes does to test a sentence) turned the note from a stray clerk's remark into a living trace of hesitation.

These small, repeated acts — the physical movement between places, the repetition of a cup, the slow transcription of ink onto my page — allow patience to do its work. Patience clarifies what the source can and cannot say; it encourages the hedges and the cautious phrases that historians owe their evidence. It also, if I'm honest, gives fiction a kind of moral ballast: to write a scene from such material is to be accountable to the rhythm of research that produced it.

So the kettle is not mere domesticity; it is part of a method. Slow rituals tidy the mind, and in the tidy room a line of marginalia looks less like a curiosity and more like a hinge on which a scene might turn.

Editor, Historical Methods

I am writing to propose an article for Historical Methods entitled “Margins as Voice: Reading Soldiers’ Marginalia in British Correspondence, 1944–45”, an approximately 7,500‑word piece that combines narrative reconstruction with methodological reflection. Dear Ms Reynolds,

I am writing to seek representation for my completed historical novel The Last Capitulation, which is 95,000 words in length. On close reading of several service files (notably folio no. 47, WO 262/193), the moment of surrender in the Dutch town of Goes presented itself as both a factual pivot and a scene that might bear fictional scrutiny and moral complication — the book follows a junior officer whose duties oblige him to record names and times even as the town appears to hold its breath and old alliances are quietly reconsidered. The novel is grounded in archival research into General Foulkes’ role in the surrender and in oral testimony gathered in Rotterdam and Goes in 2019; it would seem to sit between literary wartime fiction and tightly reconstructed military history. I attach the full manuscript and a one-page synopsis for your consideration and would be grateful for the opportunity to discuss representation at your convenience.

Yours sincerely,

Thomas Beckett

Thomas Beckett
Freelance historical novelist and archival researcher

Dear Members of the Committee,

I write to report briefly on a productive day in the archives and to request a modest allocation for digitisation. Today I consulted eight files at TNA, most notably WO 373/94, folio 8v, which contains a terse administrative note (04:15, 05-05-1945) that materially shapes my understanding of the timing of surrender negotiations. On close reading this folio suggests a procedural hesitation at the local level — an interpretive nuance that will inform a climactic chapter in the novel and will be central to a public lecture planned for October.

To proceed to a full transcription and to make the material accessible for peer review and for use in the public talk, I need to secure high-quality digital copies of approximately 300 folios. The repository's digitisation charge is £0.45 per folio, giving a total request of £135. These files will be archived with appropriate provenance notes and will be supplied to the committee in PDF format.

If I'm honest, the single folio mentioned above has already shifted my draft in ways I had not anticipated; it would seem to be worth making the entire set reproducible for both scholarly verification and for the wider public engagement that the grant anticipates.

Thank you for considering this request. I am happy to provide scanned samples or further justification if that would assist your deliberations.

With best regards,
Thomas Beckett
